```{r}
#| label: fig-tepr-timecourse
#| fig-cap: "Task-Evoked Pupil Response (TEPR) Time Course. Grand-average pupil traces (baseline-corrected, mean ± 95% CI) aligned to squeeze onset for four conditions (Easy/Low, Easy/High, Hard/Low, Hard/High), separately for ADT (top) and VDT (bottom). The shaded region indicates the cognitive AUC window used for TEPR quantification (4.65s to 7.65s relative to squeeze onset, extending from 300ms after target stimulus onset until ~3s post-target). Baseline-corrected traces converge at 0 during the baseline period (-0.5 to 0s). Vertical dashed lines indicate key events: trial start (0s), target stimulus onset (4.35s), and response signal onset (4.7s)."
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "85%"
#| echo: false
# Generate TEPR time course figure
if (!is.null(pupil_data)) {
  # Try to load waveform summary data
  waveform_file <- file.path(proj_root, "quick_share_v7/analysis/pupil_waveforms_condition_mean.csv")
  
  if (file.exists(waveform_file)) {
    waveform_data <- read_csv(waveform_file, show_col_types = FALSE)
    
    # Filter to chapter 3 data and keep all 4 conditions (effort × difficulty)
    waveform_ch3 <- waveform_data %>%
      filter(chapter == "ch3") %>%
      # Map difficulty level from stimulus_intensity and isOddball
      mutate(
        difficulty_level = case_when(
          isOddball == 0 | (is.na(isOddball) & (!is.na(stimulus_intensity) & stimulus_intensity == 0)) ~ "Standard",
          !is.na(stimulus_intensity) & stimulus_intensity %in% c(1, 2) ~ "Hard",
          !is.na(stimulus_intensity) & stimulus_intensity %in% c(3, 4) ~ "Easy",
          isOddball == 1 & is.na(stimulus_intensity) ~ "Easy",
          TRUE ~ NA_character_
        ),
        effort_level = case_when(
          effort == "Low" | effort == "Low_Force_5pct" ~ "Low",
          effort == "High" | effort == "High_Force_40pct" ~ "High",
          TRUE ~ NA_character_
        ),
        # Create condition label (Difficulty / Effort)
        condition = case_when(
          !is.na(difficulty_level) & !is.na(effort_level) ~ 
            paste0(difficulty_level, " / ", effort_level),
          TRUE ~ "Unknown"
        )
      ) %>%
      mutate(
        difficulty_level = gsub("\u2013", "-", difficulty_level),
        effort_level = gsub("\u2013", "-", effort_level),
        condition = gsub("\u2013", "-", condition)
      ) %>%
      # Filter out Standard trials (we want Easy/Hard only) and Unknown
      filter(condition != "Unknown", !grepl("Standard", condition)) %>%
      # Use mean_pupil_full (baseline-corrected, B0-corrected) - this converges at 0 in baseline period
      # Per plot_pupil_waveforms.R line 134: mean_pupil_full is the B0-corrected (full baseline correction)
      rename(mean_pupil_isolated = mean_pupil_full) %>%
      # Group by task, condition, and time to get per-condition means
      group_by(task, condition, t_rel) %>%
      summarise(
        # Weighted mean across any duplicate entries (weight by n_trials)
        total_trials = sum(n_trials, na.rm = TRUE),
        mean_pupil_isolated = sum(mean_pupil_isolated * n_trials, na.rm = TRUE) / total_trials,
        n_trials = total_trials,
        .groups = "drop"
      ) %>%
      filter(!is.na(task), !is.na(condition), !is.na(t_rel), !is.na(mean_pupil_isolated)) %>%
      arrange(task, condition, t_rel)
    
    if (nrow(waveform_ch3) > 0) {
      # Define event markers and cognitive AUC window
      # Based on Methods section: cognitive AUC window is 4.65s to 7.65s (300ms after target until 3.3s post-target)
      trial_start <- 0.0  # Trial start (squeeze onset)
      target_onset <- 4.35  # Target stimulus onset
      response_signal_onset <- 4.7  # Response signal onset
      cognitive_auc_start <- 4.65  # 300ms after target onset (4.35 + 0.3)
      cognitive_auc_end <- 7.65  # 3.3s post-target (4.35 + 3.3), which is the W3.0 window
      
      # Define color scheme for 4 conditions (matching plot_pupil_waveforms.R)
      condition_colors <- c(
        "Easy / Low" = "#5DADE2",    # Light blue
        "Easy / High" = "#2E86AB",   # Dark blue  
        "Hard / Low" = "#EC70AB",    # Light pink
        "Hard / High" = "#A23B72"    # Dark pink
      )
      
      # Get conditions actually present in data
      conditions_present <- unique(waveform_ch3$condition)
      conditions_present <- conditions_present[!is.na(conditions_present)]
      colors_for_plot <- condition_colors[names(condition_colors) %in% conditions_present]
      if (length(colors_for_plot) == 0) {
        # Fallback: use default colors if no matches
        colors_for_plot <- scales::hue_pal()(length(conditions_present))
        names(colors_for_plot) <- conditions_present
      }
      
      # Calculate y-limits from data (use full range to show all curves, add padding for labels)
      y_vals <- waveform_ch3$mean_pupil_isolated[!is.na(waveform_ch3$mean_pupil_isolated)]
      if (length(y_vals) > 0) {
        # Use full range to ensure all curves are visible
        y_range <- range(y_vals, na.rm = TRUE)
        y_range_span <- diff(y_range)
        if (!is.finite(y_range_span) || y_range_span == 0) {
          y_range_span <- max(abs(y_range), na.rm = TRUE)
          if (!is.finite(y_range_span) || y_range_span == 0) y_range_span <- 1
        }
        # Add padding (12% top, 8% bottom) to accommodate labels and ensure visibility
        y_upper_limit <- y_range[2] + y_range_span * 0.12  # Extra space for labels
        y_lower_limit <- y_range[1] - y_range_span * 0.08  # Padding at bottom
      } else {
        y_upper_limit <- 0.5
        y_lower_limit <- -0.5
        y_range_span <- 1  # Default span for label positioning
      }
      
      # Event markers with staggered y positions to avoid overlap (vertical text)
      event_markers <- tibble(
        event = c("Trial Start", "Target", "Response"),
        time = c(trial_start, target_onset, response_signal_onset),
        label_y = y_upper_limit - y_range_span * c(0.05, 0.10, 0.15)  # Stagger vertically
      )
      
      # Create plot
      p_tepr <- ggplot(waveform_ch3, aes(x = t_rel, y = mean_pupil_isolated, 
                                         color = condition, fill = condition)) +
        # Cognitive AUC window shading
        geom_rect(aes(xmin = cognitive_auc_start, xmax = cognitive_auc_end, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf),
                  inherit.aes = FALSE, fill = "grey90", alpha = 0.3) +
        # GAM smoothed lines with confidence intervals
        geom_smooth(se = TRUE, method = "gam", formula = y ~ s(x, k = 20), 
                    linewidth = 1.2, alpha = 0.3) +
        # Event markers (vertical dashed lines)
        geom_vline(data = event_markers, aes(xintercept = time), 
                   inherit.aes = FALSE, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40", linewidth = 0.6) +
        # Event labels (vertical text to avoid overlap)
        geom_text(data = event_markers, aes(x = time, y = label_y, label = event),
                  inherit.aes = FALSE, angle = 90, hjust = 0, vjust = 0.9,
                  size = 3.5, color = "grey20", fontface = "bold") +
        # Facet by task (stacked vertically)
        facet_wrap(~task, ncol = 1, labeller = labeller(task = c("ADT" = "ADT", 
                                                                  "VDT" = "VDT"))) +
        # Scales
        scale_color_manual(values = colors_for_plot, name = "Condition") +
        scale_fill_manual(values = colors_for_plot, name = "Condition") +
        scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(-0.5, 8, 1), expand = c(0, 0.1)) +
        coord_cartesian(ylim = c(y_lower_limit, y_upper_limit)) +
        # Labels and theme
        labs(
          x = "Time (s, relative to squeeze onset)",
          y = "Baseline-Corrected Pupil Diameter (AU)",
          title = NULL
        ) +
        theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
        theme(
          panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
          panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "grey90", linewidth = 0.5),
          strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
          strip.background = element_rect(fill = "grey95", color = NA),
          legend.position = "bottom",
          legend.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
          axis.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
          plot.margin = margin(10, 10, 10, 10)
        )
      
      # Print plot
      print(p_tepr)
    } else {
      # Placeholder if no data
      # Waveform data not available - ensure label still resolves
      invisible(NULL)
    }
  } else {
    # Placeholder if file not found
    # Waveform file not found - ensure label still resolves
    invisible(NULL)
  }
} else {
  # Placeholder if pupil_data not loaded - use invisible output to ensure label resolves
  invisible(NULL)
}
```

### Task modality effects

Sensitivity analyses confirmed that the Effort → Drift effect was robust to Task inclusion (Appendix~A5.3). Although auditory and visual tasks differed in absolute drift rates (Task main effect $\beta \approx 0.07$, 95% CrI [0.02, 0.12]), the Effort × Task interaction was not significant ($\beta \approx 0.03$, 95% CrI [−0.03, 0.09], includes zero), indicating that High effort reduced drift rate similarly in both modalities.

@fig-drift-by-condition shows drift rate estimates separately for ADT and VDT across all difficulty and effort conditions. The difficulty gradient (Standard $<$ Hard $<$ Easy) is consistent across both modalities, with VDT showing slightly lower absolute drift rates than ADT. Critically, the effort effect (reduction in drift under high effort) manifests similarly in both tasks, confirming that the cognitive-motor interference effect generalizes across sensory modalities.

Similarly, @fig-boundary-by-condition shows boundary separation across conditions and tasks. Difficulty strongly modulates caution (Easy $<$ Standard $<$ Hard) in both tasks, with minimal effort effects. The lack of an effort effect on boundary separation (discussed in Section 3.5.2) is consistent across both ADT and VDT, suggesting that older adults do not strategically adjust response caution under increased physical effort, regardless of sensory modality.

Full statistical results including parameter estimates and contrasts are reported in Appendix~A5.3, Table 23.

### Key Contrasts

To evaluate our a priori predictions about how effort and difficulty modulate decision parameters, we examined posterior contrasts on the link scale.

Contrasts on the link scale confirmed large effects of difficulty on drift rate ($v$), with Easy $>$ Hard $>$ Standard, and consistent effects of effort on $v$. Boundary separation ($a$) and starting-point bias ($z$) showed more modest modulation by difficulty and effort. Relative to the hypotheses in Section 1.4.1: Consistent with H1, High effort produced lower drift rates ($v$) than Low effort. Contrary to H2, boundary separation ($a$) did not reliably increase under High effort. Regarding H3 (non-decision time under High effort): We could not test H3 directly, as $t_0$ was modeled as constant across conditions for stability (see above). Exploratory models allowing $t_0$ to vary by effort showed negligible and highly uncertain effects ($\beta_{\text{effort}} = 0.02$, 95% CrI [−0.05, 0.09] on log scale, corresponding to $\Delta t_0 < 10$ ms), suggesting peripheral processes were minimally affected by the grip manipulation. Contrary to H4, starting-point bias ($z$) showed minimal effort effect (Section 3.7).

## Standard-only bias calibration on Standard trials

In a separate calibration model fit to Standard trials only, starting-point bias ($z$) was estimated independently of drift rate ($v$). Bias values were consistently above 0.5, indicating a tendency toward "different" responses. The task contrast (VDT−ADT) was $\Delta z = -0.04$, 95% CrI [−0.06, −0.02], with VDT showing *lower* bias toward "different" responses than ADT, and minimal effort effect (Low−High $\Delta z = -0.01$, 95% CrI [−0.02, 0.01]; @tbl-standard-only-bias-contrasts, @fig-bias-by-task).

Although starting-point bias consistently favored "different" responses ($z > 0.5$), the strong negative drift rates on Standard trials ($v \approx -1.1$, see @tbl-ddm-core-by-difficulty-effort) indicate that stimulus evidence reliably overcame this initial bias, leading to correct "same" responses. This pattern demonstrates the intended dissociation between *a priori* response preferences (captured by starting-point bias) and stimulus-driven evidence accumulation (captured by drift rate)—a key advantage of response-side coding over accuracy-based parameterizations.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-standard-only-bias-contrasts
#| tbl-cap: "Standard-only bias contrasts (posterior differences in $z$; $p_{>0} = P(\\Delta z > 0)$). Includes both task contrast (Visual − Auditory) and effort contrast (Low − High)."
#| tbl-pos: "htbp"
# Build bias contrasts table with dissertation-grade validation (using standardized column names)
tbl_bias_contr_raw <- std_bias_contrasts %>%
  filter(threshold == PRIMARY_THR, rt_type == PRIMARY_RT)

# DISSERTATION-GRADE VALIDATION: Stop if any CI columns are missing
if (anyNA(tbl_bias_contr_raw$q2.5) || anyNA(tbl_bias_contr_raw$q97.5)) {
  missing_q2.5 <- sum(is.na(tbl_bias_contr_raw$q2.5))
  missing_q97.5 <- sum(is.na(tbl_bias_contr_raw$q97.5))
  broken_rows <- tbl_bias_contr_raw %>%
    filter(is.na(q2.5) | is.na(q97.5)) %>%
    select(contrast, estimate, q2.5, q97.5, p_gt0)
  
  stop("standard_only_bias_contrasts.csv has NA credible intervals. Re-run postprocess step.\n",
       "  Missing q2.5: ", missing_q2.5, " rows\n",
       "  Missing q97.5: ", missing_q97.5, " rows\n",
       "  Broken rows:\n",
       paste(capture.output(print(broken_rows)), collapse = "\n"),
       call. = FALSE)
}

# Build display table - include ALL contrasts (no filtering; use manuscript-ready labels)
tbl_bias_contr <- tbl_bias_contr_raw %>%
  select(contrast, estimate, q2.5, q97.5, p_gt0) %>%
  mutate(
    contrast = format_contrast_display(contrast),
    estimate = round(estimate, 3),
    q2.5 = round(q2.5, 3),
    q97.5 = round(q97.5, 3),
    p_gt0 = round(p_gt0, 3),
    `95% CrI` = paste0("[", q2.5, ", ", q97.5, "]")
  ) %>%
  select(contrast, estimate, `95% CrI`, p_gt0) %>%
  rename(
    `Contrast` = contrast,
    `Δz` = estimate,
    `P(Δz > 0)` = p_gt0
  )

message(sprintf("Bias contrasts table: %d rows (should include both Task and Effort contrasts)", nrow(tbl_bias_contr)))

tbl_bias_contr %>%
  knitr::kable(format = ifelse(knitr::is_latex_output(), "latex", "html"), 
               booktabs = TRUE, 
               linesep = "",
               align = c("l", "r", "l", "r")) %>%
  kableExtra::kable_styling(
    latex_options = c("striped", "hold_position"),
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed", "responsive"),
    full_width = FALSE
  )
```


### Integrated Condition Effects

To summarize how difficulty and effort jointly influenced all DDM parameters, @fig-integrated-condition-effects shows integrated condition effects on $a$, $z$, and $t_0$. Difficulty effects were strongest for boundary separation ($a$), with Easy trials showing reduced caution relative to Hard trials. Effort effects were smaller and most evident for $t_0$, where High effort produced longer non-decision times. Bias ($z$) varied by task and effort but not by difficulty, consistent with the design constraints described in the Methods.

```{r}
#| label: fig-integrated-condition-effects
#| fig-pos: "htbp"
#| fig-cap: "Integrated condition effects on DDM parameters $v$, $a$, and $z$. Multi-panel forest plot showing posterior means with 95% credible intervals for difficulty and effort effects on drift rate ($v$), boundary separation ($a$), and starting-point bias ($z$). Bias ($z$) does not vary by difficulty (see Methods)."
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "70%"
#| fig-height: 10
# Dynamic: from fixef_link (run_dir)
if (!is.null(fixef_link) && nrow(fixef_link) > 0) {
  fx_int <- fixef_link %>%
    filter(model == PRIMARY_MODEL, rt_type == PRIMARY_RT) %>%
    filter(!grepl("^ndt_", term), term != "Intercept", !grepl("^bs_Intercept$|^bias_Intercept$", term)) %>%
    mutate(
      param_type = case_when(
        grepl("^bs_", term) ~ "Boundary (a)",
        grepl("^bias_", term) ~ "Bias (z)",
        grepl("^b_", term) | (!grepl("^bs_|^bias_", term) & grepl("Intercept", term)) ~ "Drift (v)",
        TRUE ~ "Drift (v)"
      ),
      term_clean = case_when(
        grepl("difficulty_3Hard", term) ~ "Hard vs Standard",
        grepl("difficulty_3Easy", term) ~ "Easy vs Standard",
        grepl("effort_conditionhigh", term) ~ "High vs Low",
        grepl("taskVDT", term) ~ "VDT vs ADT",
        TRUE ~ gsub("difficulty_3|effort_condition|bias_|bs_", "", term)
      )
    ) %>%
    filter(term_clean %in% c("Hard vs Standard", "Easy vs Standard", "High vs Low", "VDT vs ADT"))
  if (nrow(fx_int) > 0) {
    p_int <- ggplot(fx_int, aes(x = Estimate, y = term_clean)) +
      geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray60", linewidth = 0.5) +
      geom_point(aes(color = param_type), size = 2.5) +
      geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = Q2.5, xmax = Q97.5, color = param_type), height = 0.2, linewidth = 1) +
      facet_wrap(~ param_type, scales = "free_x", ncol = 1) +
      scale_color_manual(values = c("Drift (v)" = "#2E86AB", "Boundary (a)" = "#A23B72", "Bias (z)" = "#28A745")) +
      labs(title = "Integrated Condition Effects on DDM Parameters",
           subtitle = "Posterior means with 95% credible intervals (link scale). Effects identical across ADT and VDT.",
           x = "Effect Estimate (95% CrI)", y = "Condition", color = "Parameter") +
      theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
      theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 13, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
            plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, hjust = 0.5, color = "gray60"),
            strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10), legend.position = "bottom",
            panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
    print(p_int)
  } else {
include_graphics_safe(fig_path("fig_integrated_condition_effects.pdf"))
  }
} else {
  include_graphics_safe(fig_path("fig_integrated_condition_effects.pdf"))
}
```

### Individual Differences

The hierarchical structure revealed substantial individual differences in all DDM parameters, with drift rate showing the widest variability. Parameter correlations revealed a weak negative relationship ($r$ = −0.205) between drift intercept and bias intercept at the subject level. Supporting figures are provided in Appendix~A1 (@fig-subject-parameter-distribution and @fig-brinley-plot).

## Pupil-linked modulation of decision parameters {#sec-pupil-ddm-integration}

We next tested whether trial-by-trial phasic pupil responses (TEPR-based, z-scored within participant) modulated drift rate ($v$) or starting-point bias ($z$) in the DDM.

Pupil-augmented models were fit only to trials with valid pupil data (N $\approx$ 12,000 trials). To enable fair LOO comparison, the behavioral-only baseline was refit on this same pupil-available subset. LOOIC values in @tbl-pupil-loo reflect predictive performance on the shared dataset; they are not comparable to Table 7 models (which used the full N = 18,097 trial dataset).

Model comparison via LOO showed large apparent differences ($\Delta$LOOIC $\approx$ 12,900; @tbl-pupil-loo), but with high Pareto-$k$ diagnostics (max $k$ = 0.91), indicating PSIS-LOO estimates are unreliable for these data. We therefore interpret pupil effects cautiously based on posterior parameter estimates rather than model selection criteria. Trial-wise pupil coefficients on $v$ and $z$ had posterior means near zero with 95% CrIs encompassing zero (@tbl-pupil-key-effects), consistent with no clear modulation of evidence accumulation or starting-point bias by phasic pupil responses. Full fixed effects for pupil predictors are provided in Appendix~A6 (Section 5.5) and the online supplement. Several factors may contribute to these null pupil-DDM associations. First, the W3.0 time window (0–3 s post-probe) may have captured post-decisional pupil dynamics in addition to pre-decision arousal, potentially masking trial-to-trial relationships with evidence accumulation. Second, baseline pupil diameter differed modestly by effort condition (@tbl-baseline-pupil), though the functional significance of this difference is unclear without formal inferential testing; individual differences in phasic pupil responses may have obscured systematic trial-level modulation of decision parameters. Finally, the pupil-boundary relationship reported by Cavanagh et al. [-@cavanagh2014] emerged in a probabilistic learning task with explicit conflict signals, whereas our perceptual discrimination paradigm may not generate the same conflict-driven arousal signatures.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-pupil-loo
#| tbl-cap: "Model comparison for pupil-augmented DDMs (within pupil-available trials). Note. Pareto-$k$ diagnostics (max $k$ = 0.91) indicate PSIS-LOO estimates may be unreliable for these models. Model comparison should be interpreted cautiously; we rely primarily on posterior parameter estimates rather than LOO-based selection."
#| tbl-pos: "htbp"

pupil_loo_file <- file.path(proj_root, "output", "pupil_ddm", "tables", "pupil_loo_summary.csv")

}

if (file.exists(pupil_loo_file)) {
  pupil_loo <- read_csv(pupil_loo_file, show_col_types = FALSE)
  # Map script names to reader-friendly labels; handle both model_name and model columns
  model_col <- if ("model_name" %in% names(pupil_loo)) "model_name" else "model"
  model_labels <- c(
    "model_0_behavioral" = "Behavioral only",
    "model_1_pupil_bias" = "Pupil on bias (z)",
    "model_2_pupil_bias_drift" = "Pupil on bias + drift (v, z)"
  )
  pupil_loo_display <- pupil_loo %>%
    mutate(
      Model = coalesce(model_labels[.data[[model_col]]], gsub("_", " ", .data[[model_col]])),
      across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 2))
    ) %>%
    select(-all_of(model_col)) %>%
    relocate(Model, .before = 1) %>%
    rename(
      `ELPD (LOO)` = elpd_loo,
      `SE(ELPD)` = se_elpd_loo,
      `LOOIC` = looic,
      `SE(LOOIC)` = looic_se,
      `Max Pareto k` = pareto_k_max,
      `ΔELPD` = delta_elpd,
      `ΔLOOIC` = delta_looic
    )
  pupil_loo_display %>%
    knitr::kable(format = ifelse(knitr::is_latex_output(), "latex", "html"),

      full_width = FALSE
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-pupil-key-effects
#| tbl-cap: "Key pupil effects on drift ($v$) and bias ($z$) (link scale). Posterior mean, 95% CrI, and whether the interval includes zero."
#| tbl-pos: "htbp"

pupil_key_terms_file <- file.path(proj_root, "output", "pupil_ddm", "tables", "pupil_effects_key_terms.csv")
if (!file.exists(pupil_key_terms_file)) {
  pupil_key_terms_file <- file.path(proj_root, "output", "ddm_pupil", "tables", "pupil_effects_key_terms.csv")
}

if (file.exists(pupil_key_terms_file)) {
  pupil_key_terms <- read_csv(pupil_key_terms_file, show_col_types = FALSE)
  cn <- names(pupil_key_terms)
  est_col <- intersect(c("Estimate", "estimate", "mean"), cn)[1]
  q2_col <- intersect(c("Q2.5", "q2.5", "q_2.5"), cn)[1]
  q97_col <- intersect(c("Q97.5", "q97.5", "q_97.5"), cn)[1]
  term_col <- intersect(c("term", "parameter", "Parameter"), cn)[1]
  if (is.na(est_col)) est_col <- cn[1]
  if (is.na(term_col)) term_col <- cn[1]
  if (!is.na(q2_col) && !is.na(q97_col) && q2_col %in% cn && q97_col %in% cn) {
    pupil_key_terms_display <- pupil_key_terms %>%
      mutate(
        mean = round(.data[[est_col]], 3),
        `95% CrI` = paste0("[", round(.data[[q2_col]], 3), ", ", round(.data[[q97_col]], 3), "]"),
        `Includes 0` = ifelse(.data[[q2_col]] <= 0 & .data[[q97_col]] >= 0, "Yes", "No"),
        term_display = case_when(
          "dpar" %in% cn & .data[["dpar"]] == "v" ~ "Pupil $v$",
          "dpar" %in% cn & .data[["dpar"]] == "bias" ~ "Pupil $z$",
          grepl("drift", .data[[term_col]], ignore.case = TRUE) & !grepl("bias", .data[[term_col]], ignore.case = TRUE) ~ "Pupil $v$",
          grepl("bias", .data[[term_col]], ignore.case = TRUE) ~ "Pupil $z$",
          TRUE ~ as.character(.data[[term_col]])
        )
      ) %>%
      # Keep one row per parameter type (deduplicate): first row per v/z
      group_by(term_display) %>%
      slice(1) %>%
      ungroup() %>%
      arrange(factor(term_display, levels = c("Pupil $v$", "Pupil $z$"))) %>%
      select(term_display, mean, `95% CrI`, `Includes 0`) %>%
      rename(Parameter = term_display)
  } else {
  pupil_key_terms_display <- pupil_key_terms %>%
    mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3)))
  }
  kbl_args <- list(
    format = ifelse(knitr::is_latex_output(), "latex", "html"),
                 booktabs = TRUE,
                 linesep = "",
    digits = 3
  )
  if (knitr::is_latex_output()) {
    kbl_args$escape <- FALSE
    kbl_args$col.names <- c("Parameter", "Mean", "95\\% CrI", "Includes 0")
  }
  do.call(knitr::kable, c(list(pupil_key_terms_display), kbl_args)) %>%
    kableExtra::kable_styling(
      latex_options = c("striped", "hold_position"),
      bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed", "responsive"),
      full_width = FALSE
    )
} else {

}
```

## Sensitivity analysis across RT cutoffs

Parameter estimates were robust across RT cutoff thresholds (0.15, 0.20, 0.25 s), with 95% CrI overlap for all key contrasts (Appendix~A5.2, @tbl-sensitivity-thresholds). We adopted 0.20 s as the primary cutoff, balancing exclusion of fast guesses with trial retention.

Because different RT cutoffs exclude different numbers of trials, raw LOOIC values are **not directly comparable** across thresholds (@tbl-sensitivity-thresholds). LOOIC is a measure of total log predictive density, which scales with sample size. We therefore evaluate sensitivity by comparing **parameter estimates** and **effect directions** across cutoffs, not by selecting the "best" LOOIC model.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sensitivity-thresholds
#| tbl-cap: "Sensitivity to minimum cue-locked RT cutoff (0.15/0.20/0.25 s)."
#| tbl-pos: "htbp"
# Build sensitivity table from tbl_sens (handle optional LOOIC columns)
# Build column list dynamically
cols_to_select <- c("threshold", "n_trials")
if ("looic" %in% names(tbl_sens)) {
  cols_to_select <- c(cols_to_select, "looic")
}
if ("looic_se" %in% names(tbl_sens)) {
  cols_to_select <- c(cols_to_select, "looic_se")
}

tbl_sens_base <- tbl_sens %>%
  select(all_of(cols_to_select)) %>%
  arrange(threshold)

# Add LOOIC columns if they don't exist
if (!"looic" %in% names(tbl_sens_base)) {
  tbl_sens_base <- tbl_sens_base %>% mutate(looic = NA_real_)
}
if (!"looic_se" %in% names(tbl_sens_base)) {
  tbl_sens_base <- tbl_sens_base %>% mutate(looic_se = NA_real_)
}

tbl_sens_compact <- tbl_sens_base %>%
  mutate(
    looic = if (!all(is.na(looic))) round(looic, 1) else NA_real_,
    looic_se = if (!all(is.na(looic_se))) round(looic_se, 1) else NA_real_,
    n_trials = format(n_trials, big.mark = ",")
  ) %>%
  select(threshold, n_trials, looic, looic_se) %>%
  rename(
    `Threshold (s)` = threshold,
    `N trials` = n_trials,
    `LOOIC` = looic,
    `LOOIC SE` = looic_se
  )

tbl_sens_compact %>%
  knitr::kable(format = ifelse(knitr::is_latex_output(), "latex", "html"), 
               booktabs = TRUE, 
               linesep = "") %>%
  kableExtra::kable_styling(
    latex_options = c("striped", "hold_position"),
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed", "responsive"),
    full_width = FALSE
  )
```

Parameter estimates and the pattern of effects on $v$, $a$, $t_0$, and $z$ were qualitatively stable across cutoffs (Appendix~A5.2). The key finding—that High effort reduces drift rate—is robust across all three RT cutoffs, indicating the conclusion is not driven by fast or premature responses. We adopted 0.20 s as the primary cutoff, balancing exclusion of fast guesses with trial retention (@tbl-sensitivity-thresholds).

# Discussion

## Summary of Key Findings

Results confirmed Hypothesis 1 (H1): High effort reduced drift rate, consistent with resource competition or supra-optimal arousal (Section 4.2). Contrary to Hypothesis 2 (H2), boundary separation did not increase under High effort, contradicting conflict-control predictions (Section 4.4). Hypothesis 3 (H3) could not be tested directly due to model constraints requiring constant $t_0$, though exploratory analyses suggested minimal peripheral slowing (Section 4.3). Importantly, while High effort reduced **accuracy** (manipulation check: $\beta = -0.15$, $p < .001$), it did not reliably slow **reaction time** ($\beta = 0.02$ s, 95% CI [−0.02, 0.05]). This dissociation—lower accuracy without RT slowing—is explained by the DDM decomposition: drift rate declined (evidence quality), but boundary separation did not increase (no compensatory caution), resulting in faster errors rather than slower correct responses. The Effort → Drift effect was robust to Task (ADT vs. VDT) inclusion (Appendix~A5.3). Trial-wise pupil-linked arousal (TEPR) did not reliably modulate drift rate or starting-point bias when included as predictors (Section 3.8). This pattern of results confirms the "detrimental impact" hypothesis grounded in Resource Competition theory [@azer2023; @wickens2008], which predicts that concurrent physical effort consumes shared cognitive resources, degrading the quality of evidence accumulation. However, the null effect on boundary separation challenges the "adaptive caution" hypothesis (Strategic Adaptation), which predicted that older adults would respond to increased internal noise by raising their decision thresholds to preserve accuracy.

## The "Crunch Point": Why Drift Rate Declined

Our finding that High physical effort significantly reduced drift rates—indicating slower and noisier information accumulation—challenges simple arousal-facilitation accounts and aligns more closely with resource-depletion models. Specifically, the observed decline in processing efficiency supports the **Compensation-Related Utilization of Neural Circuits Hypothesis (CRUNCH)** [@reuterlorenz2008]. The CRUNCH model posits that while older adults can effectively recruit compensatory neural resources to meet lower task demands, they hit a resource ceiling or "crunch point" at lower levels of objective difficulty than younger adults. Once this threshold is crossed, compensatory mechanisms fail, and performance declines precipitously. In the present study, the 40% MVC condition likely pushed participants beyond this critical tipping point. Rather than acting as a beneficial arousal boost that "sharpens" neural gain (as predicted by Adaptive Gain Theory for moderate levels; [@astonjones2005]), the sustained High-effort requirement consumed the limited cognitive resources available for evidence accumulation, resulting in the observed degradation of drift rate.

```{r}
#| label: fig-decision-landscape
#| fig-cap: "The Decision Landscape: Effect of Drift Rate on RT Distribution. This 3D surface visualizes the theoretical 'Crunch Point' observed in our data. The vertical axis (Z) represents the probability density of a response. As drift rate ($v$, Y-axis) decreases from Easy levels ($\\approx 2.0$) to Hard/Standard levels ($\\approx 0$ to $-1.0$), the sharp peak of timely responses collapses into a flat, spread-out distribution. This visualizes why older adults' reaction times become disproportionately variable and slow when physical effort or task difficulty degrades the quality of evidence accumulation ($v$)."
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-pos: "htbp"
#| out-width: "75%"
include_graphics_safe(fig_path("fig_decision_landscape_3d.png"))
```

## Modeling Constraints: Non-Decision Time and Peripheral Processes

We initially hypothesized (H3) that concurrent grip maintenance would slow peripheral processes (perceptual encoding and motor execution), increasing non-decision time ($t_0$). However, preliminary model comparisons revealed that condition-specific $t_0$ estimates were poorly identified in our response-signal design, necessitating an intercept-only specification ($t_0 = 0.347$ s constant across conditions).

Several design factors contributed to this constraint:

1. **Brief stimulus durations (100 ms)** left minimal variance in encoding time across conditions, making perceptual delays difficult to estimate separately from decision-related slowing.

2. **Post-stimulus grip release**: Participants relaxed their grip immediately after probe offset and before the response window opened, removing direct motor interference during response execution. The 3-second response window began after grip release, meaning motor processes during the actual button press were not confounded with grip force.

3. **Response-signal timing**: The probe-onset-locked RT definition includes a fixed 0.35-s delay (0.1 s probe + 0.25 s grip-relaxation period) before the response window, but this delay is constant across conditions. Any effort-related encoding differences would need to manifest within the 100-ms stimulus window, which may be too brief to detect reliably.

4. **Model identification**: Exploratory models with `ndt ~ 1 + effort_condition` showed weak convergence (R̂ > 1.05 for effort slopes) and LOO comparison disfavored this specification ($\Delta$LOO = 12.3, SE = 5.2), indicating the data were insufficient to distinguish $t_0$ variation from trial-level noise.

Importantly, the **accuracy decline** under High effort observed in behavioral analyses (@tbl-accuracy-glmm) was fully captured by reductions in drift rate ($v$), not by changes in $t_0$. RT did not reliably slow under High effort in manipulation checks (@tbl-rt-lmm, $\beta = 0.02$ s, 95% CI [−0.02, 0.05]). This pattern suggests that cognitive-motor interference manifested during evidence accumulation—the core decision process—rather than during peripheral encoding or motor stages. This interpretation aligns with resource competition theories [@wickens2008], which posit that concurrent physical and cognitive demands compete for shared central processing resources, degrading the quality of evidence extraction rather than slowing sensory or motor transmission.

While we cannot rule out small $t_0$ effects below our detection threshold (< 10 ms), the dominance of drift rate changes indicates that the primary locus of effort-induced slowing was computational (evidence accumulation), not peripheral. Future studies using longer stimulus durations or continuous response paradigms (without post-stimulus grip release) may better isolate peripheral timing effects.

## Strategic Rigidity: Why Caution ($a$) Didn't Increase

Despite the internal noise introduced by High effort (as evidenced by reduced drift rates), older adults failed to dynamically adjust their decision criteria by increasing boundary separation ($a$). This null finding suggests *strategic rigidity* in aging: older adults may have difficulty flexibly modulating their decision thresholds in response to changing task demands, even when such adaptation would be beneficial. This rigidity could reflect reduced executive flexibility or a tendency to maintain a fixed "safety-first" strategy regardless of context. While older adults are generally risk-averse and prioritize accuracy [@starns2010], the failure to increase caution under conditions of degraded evidence quality may indicate that the cognitive resources needed for strategic adjustment are themselves depleted by the dual-task demands of the High-effort condition.

An alternative (though not mutually exclusive) explanation is that the response-signal design may have constrained participants' ability to flexibly modulate decision boundaries. The fixed post-stimulus delay (0.35 s) before the response prompt appeared may have encouraged a "wait-for-cue" strategy that overrode spontaneous boundary adjustments. Notably, our boundary estimates varied by stimulus-driven difficulty (Easy: 2.37, Standard: 2.41, Hard: 2.65; @tbl-ddm-core-by-difficulty-effort) but not by effortful arousal, suggesting that bottom-up perceptual factors influenced boundary setting while top-down strategic adjustments may have been suppressed by the response-signal structure. Future work using free-response paradigms (without response cues) could better isolate strategic flexibility from design-imposed temporal constraints.

## Bias and Phasic Arousal

Regarding starting-point bias ($z$), our results revealed a consistent conservative bias across conditions, with a posterior mean of $z = 0.63$ (95% CrI [0.58, 0.68]) on Standard trials, indicating a slight preference for "different" responses (@tbl-standard-only-bias-levels). This bias was robust across effort conditions, with no significant effect of effort level (High vs. Low contrast: $\Delta = -0.01$, 95% CrI [−0.02, 0.01], $p(\Delta>0) = .27$). However, we did observe a significant task difference: VDT showed less bias toward "different" than ADT ($\Delta = -0.04$, 95% CrI [−0.06, −0.02], $p(\Delta>0) < .001$; @tbl-standard-only-bias-contrasts), suggesting modality-specific differences in response tendencies.

These findings can be interpreted in the context of LC-NE system dynamics. Recent work suggests that phasic arousal, indexed by pupil dilation, can suppress pre-existing choice biases, "resetting" the decision process to a neutral state [@degee2020pupil]. The lack of a significant effort effect on bias suggests that the High-effort manipulation (40% MVC) may not have elicited strong enough phasic arousal responses to modulate starting-point bias, or that any such effects were offset by other factors. Alternatively, the integrity of the LC-NE system in our older adult sample may have moderated the expected bias suppression [@huang2024]. The task-specific bias differences (VDT < ADT) may reflect inherent differences in how auditory versus visual detection tasks engage response strategies, independent of arousal state. Direct pupillometry integration (@sec-pupil-ddm-integration) did not reveal reliable modulation of bias or drift rate by trial-wise TEPR, consistent with the null pupil-DDM associations reported in Section 3.8.

## Limitations and Future Directions

Our findings must be interpreted within the constraints of the response-signal design, where RTs are measured from response-screen onset rather than stimulus onset. This design constrains the interpretation of $t_0$ to primarily reflect motor execution and response selection, excluding early perceptual/encoding processes. Despite these constraints, our results provide clear evidence that effort regulation is critical for older adults because they have a lower "tipping point" where effort becomes interference. The CRUNCH model and CMI framework together explain why the 40% MVC condition pushed older adults past their compensatory capacity, resulting in degraded processing efficiency (reduced drift), without the adaptive increase in caution that might have mitigated these effects. (Non-decision time $t_0$ could not be tested for condition effects due to model stability constraints; see Section 4.3.) These findings underscore the importance of managing effort levels in real-world contexts where older adults must balance physical and cognitive demands.

### Model Family Limitations

1.  **Constant-drift Wiener DDM**: The base Wiener DDM assumes constant drift within each trial and no across-trial variability in drift (sv), starting point (sz), or non-decision time (s$t_0$). This can underfit fast tails, especially in VDT-Hard conditions. The constant-drift Wiener DDM underfits fast RT tails, especially in VDT-Hard. Response-signal timing limits identifiability of across-trial variability. Future work could add a small contaminant mixture, across-trial variability (sv, sz), or urgency/collapsing bounds; LBA/race models may better capture fast-tail dynamics in the Easy/VDT regime.

2.  **Non-decision time ($t_0$) intercept-only**: In the response-signal design, $t_0$ primarily reflects motor execution. We constrained $t_0$ to be constant across conditions (intercept-only) due to poor identification of condition-specific estimates in pilot models (see Results Section 3.6 and Discussion Section 4.3). This precluded testing Hypothesis 3 (effort effects on peripheral processes).

3.  **Alternative model families**: Linear Ballistic Accumulator (LBA) or race models may provide better fit for fast-tail dynamics, particularly for Easy/VDT. These models allow for more flexible RT distributions and may better accommodate the response-signal design.

### Design-Specific Limitations

4.  **Response-signal RT measurement**: RTs are measured from response-screen onset, not stimulus onset. This constrains the interpretation of $t_0$ to motor execution and response selection, excluding early perceptual/encoding processes. While this is appropriate for the current design, it limits generalizability to traditional RT paradigms.

5.  **Effort manipulation**: Physical effort (grip force) may interact with motor execution in complex ways not fully captured by small fixed effects on $t_0$. Future work integrating EMG or kinematic measures could provide richer insights into effort-motor interactions.

### Misfit in Easy/VDT

6.  **Fast-tail misfit**: The most pronounced misfit occurs in Easy/VDT conditions, where the model underpredicts the frequency of very fast correct responses. This suggests a subset of trials may reflect:

    -   Anticipatory responses (partially captured by 2% censoring)
    -   A "fast-guess" process not represented in the base DDM
    -   Extremely high drift rates that are incompatible with the assumed Wiener process for a small subset of trials

    Sensitivity analyses (2% censoring, unconditional PPCs) confirm that substantive conclusions are robust, but future work should explore mixture models or urgency signals to better account for these fast responses.

### LOO Reliability for Pupil Models

7.  **PSIS-LOO reliability for pupil-augmented models**: Pareto-k diagnostics indicated that PSIS-LOO was unreliable for pupil-augmented models ($k_{\max}$ = 0.91), likely due to influential observations where pupil responses were highly variable. This prevented definitive model comparison via LOO; future work should employ k-fold cross-validation or moment matching to obtain more stable estimates. Importantly, our conclusions about pupil effects are based on posterior parameter estimates (where TEPR coefficients were near-zero with wide credible intervals) rather than on LOO-based model selection.

8.  **TEPR window sensitivity**: We did not test sensitivity to TEPR window definition (e.g., W1.3 early window excluding motor-confounded periods) in the pupil-DDM coupling models; primary analyses used W3.0 only.


## Conclusions

This chapter presents a comprehensive hierarchical Wiener DDM analysis of a response-signal change-detection task in older adults. The primary model, in which task difficulty modulates drift rate and boundary separation, with starting-point bias constant across difficulty levels (reflecting the randomized trial design), is strongly supported by LOO cross-validation and shows acceptable fit to subject-wise mid-body RT quantiles (see Appendix~A3 (Sections A3.1 and A3.2) for full diagnostics, including @fig-ch3app-ppc-rt-overlay). Key findings—difficulty effects on $v$ and $a$; task-specific differences in bias ($z$); and small effort effects—are robust across multiple sensitivity analyses. While the base Wiener DDM shows localized misfit in fast tails (especially Easy/VDT), this does not undermine the core substantive conclusions. Future extensions incorporating across-trial variability, urgency, or mixture models may further improve absolute fit.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ndt-prior-posterior
#| fig-cap: "$t_0$ Prior vs Posterior. Prior (gray line) and posterior (blue shaded density) distributions for the $t_0$ intercept. The prior is Normal(log(0.23), 0.12) on the log scale (approximately 0.23 s on natural scale). This figure documents prior influence for the response-signal design, where $t_0$ primarily reflects motor execution rather than encoding time."
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "80%"
# Dynamic: from model in run_dir when brms available
model_path <- file.path(proj_root, params$run_dir, "models", "additive__probe_onset_locked__thr0.20.rds")
if (file.exists(model_path) && requireNamespace("brms", quietly = TRUE) && requireNamespace("posterior", quietly = TRUE)) {
  tryCatch({
    suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(brms); library(posterior) })
    fit_ndt <- readRDS(model_path)
    draws <- as_draws_df(fit_ndt, variable = "^b_ndt_", regex = TRUE)
    if (ncol(draws) > 0 && "b_ndt_Intercept" %in% names(draws)) {
      ndt_draws <- draws %>% pull(b_ndt_Intercept)
      ndt_prior <- tibble(x_log = seq(log(0.1), log(0.4), length.out = 400),
                          d = dnorm(x_log, mean = log(0.23), sd = 0.12), type = "Prior") %>%
        mutate(x_natural = exp(x_log))
      post_df <- tibble(x_log = as.numeric(ndt_draws)) %>%
        mutate(x_natural = exp(x_log), type = "Posterior")
      p_ndt <- ggplot() +
        geom_line(data = ndt_prior, aes(x = x_natural, y = d, color = "Prior"), alpha = 0.7, linewidth = 0.8) +
        geom_density(data = post_df, aes(x = x_natural, color = "Posterior", fill = "Posterior"), linewidth = 0.8, alpha = 0.3) +
        scale_color_manual(name = NULL, values = c("Prior" = "gray50", "Posterior" = "steelblue")) +
        scale_fill_manual(name = NULL, values = c("Posterior" = "steelblue"), guide = "none") +
        labs(x = "t0 (s)", y = "Density", title = "NDT Intercept: Prior vs Posterior",
             subtitle = "Prior: Normal(log(0.23), 0.12) on log scale") +
        theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
        theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
              plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9, color = "gray50", hjust = 0.5), legend.position = "top")
      print(p_ndt)
    } else {
include_graphics_safe(fig_path("fig_ndt_prior_posterior.pdf"))
    }
  }, error = function(e) {
    include_graphics_safe(fig_path("fig_ndt_prior_posterior.pdf"))
  })
} else {
  include_graphics_safe(fig_path("fig_ndt_prior_posterior.pdf"))
}
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-convergence-ppc-gate-appendix
#| tbl-cap: "Convergence & PPC Gate (Primary Model). See Results Section 3.4 for summary."
#| tbl-pos: "htbp"
# Prefer run_dir convergence (matches main DDM data); fallback to publish_gate for conv and PPC
conv_primary_row <- tbl_convergence %>%
  filter(model == PRIMARY_MODEL, rt_type == PRIMARY_RT, threshold == PRIMARY_THR) %>%
  slice(1)
conv_max_rhat   <- if (nrow(conv_primary_row) > 0) conv_primary_row$max_rhat   else (if (!is.null(publish_gate)) publish_gate$conv_max_rhat   else NA_real_)
conv_min_bulk   <- if (nrow(conv_primary_row) > 0) conv_primary_row$min_bulk_ess else (if (!is.null(publish_gate)) publish_gate$conv_min_bulk_ess else NA_real_)
conv_min_tail   <- if (!is.null(publish_gate) && !is.na(publish_gate$conv_min_tail_ess)) publish_gate$conv_min_tail_ess else NA_real_  # run_dir has no tail ESS
conv_div        <- if (nrow(conv_primary_row) > 0) conv_primary_row$n_divergent else (if (!is.null(publish_gate)) publish_gate$conv_divergences else NA_integer_)
conv_pass       <- !is.na(conv_max_rhat) && conv_max_rhat < 1.01 && !is.na(conv_min_bulk) && conv_min_bulk >= 400 && !is.na(conv_div) && conv_div == 0
ppc_n_cells     <- if (!is.null(publish_gate)) publish_gate$ppc_subj_n_cells     else NA_real_
ppc_pct_flagged <- if (!is.null(publish_gate)) publish_gate$ppc_subj_pct_flagged_any else NA_real_
ppc_max_qp      <- if (!is.null(publish_gate)) publish_gate$ppc_subj_max_qp     else NA_real_
ppc_max_ks      <- if (!is.null(publish_gate)) publish_gate$ppc_subj_max_ks      else NA_real_
ppc_pass        <- if (!is.null(publish_gate)) publish_gate$ppc_subj_pass        else NA
if (!is.null(publish_gate) || nrow(conv_primary_row) > 0) {
  gate_tbl <- tibble(
    Metric = c(
      "Max R-hat", "Min Bulk ESS", "Min Tail ESS", "Divergences",
      "Convergence Pass", "PPC Cells (n)", "PPC Flagged (%)",
      "Max QP RMSE (s)", "Max KS", "PPC Pass"
    ),
    Value = c(
      ifelse(is.na(conv_max_rhat), "—", sprintf("%.4f", conv_max_rhat)),
      ifelse(is.na(conv_min_bulk), "—", sprintf("%.0f", conv_min_bulk)),
      ifelse(is.na(conv_min_tail), "—", sprintf("%.0f", conv_min_tail)),
      as.character(ifelse(is.na(conv_div), "—", conv_div)),
      ifelse(is.na(conv_pass), "—", ifelse(conv_pass, "✓", "✗")),
      ifelse(is.na(ppc_n_cells), "—", sprintf("%.0f", ppc_n_cells)),
      ifelse(is.na(ppc_pct_flagged), "—", sprintf("%.1f%%", ppc_pct_flagged)),
      ifelse(is.na(ppc_max_qp), "—", sprintf("%.3f", ppc_max_qp)),
      ifelse(is.na(ppc_max_ks), "—", sprintf("%.3f", ppc_max_ks)),
      ifelse(is.na(ppc_pass), "—", ifelse(ppc_pass, "✓", "✗"))
    )
  )
  gate_tbl %>% gt() %>%
    tab_style(style = cell_text(weight = "bold"), locations = cells_column_labels()) %>%
    tab_style(style = cell_text(style = "italic"), locations = cells_body(columns = Metric)) %>%
    cols_width(Metric ~ px(180), Value ~ px(100)) %>% opt_table_font(size = "small")
} else {
  invisible(NULL)
}
```

## A2. Individual Differences and Parameter Relationships {.unnumbered}

```{r}
#| label: fig-subject-parameter-distribution
#| fig-cap: "Subject-Level Parameter Distribution. Violin plots showing the distribution of subject-level random effects (deviations from group mean) for each DDM parameter. The boxplots within each violin show the median and interquartile range. Zero (dashed line) represents the group mean. This visualization highlights the substantial individual variability in decision-making parameters across our sample of 67 older adults."
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-pos: "htbp"
#| out-width: "75%"
# Dynamic: from model ranef when brms available
model_path_re <- file.path(proj_root, params$run_dir, "models", "additive__probe_onset_locked__thr0.20.rds")
if (file.exists(model_path_re) && requireNamespace("brms", quietly = TRUE)) {
  tryCatch({
    suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(brms))
    fit_re <- readRDS(model_path_re)
    re <- ranef(fit_re)
    if (!is.null(re) && "subject_id" %in% names(re)) {
      re_subj <- re$subject_id
      par_names <- dimnames(re_subj)[[3]]
      re_list <- list()
      for (par in par_names) {
        if ("Estimate" %in% dimnames(re_subj)[[2]]) {
          re_est <- re_subj[, "Estimate", par]
          re_list[[length(re_list) + 1]] <- tibble(subject_id = names(re_est), parameter = par, estimate = as.numeric(re_est))
        }
      }
      if (length(re_list) > 0) {
      re_df <- bind_rows(re_list) %>%
        mutate(
          parameter = case_when(
            parameter == "Intercept" | (grepl("Intercept", parameter) & !grepl("bias|bs|ndt", parameter)) ~ "Drift (v)",
            grepl("bs_|boundary", parameter, ignore.case = TRUE) ~ "Boundary (a)",
            grepl("bias", parameter, ignore.case = TRUE) ~ "Bias (z)",
            grepl("ndt", parameter, ignore.case = TRUE) ~ "Non-decision time (t0)",
            TRUE ~ parameter
          )
        )
      re_df$parameter <- factor(re_df$parameter, levels = c("Drift (v)", "Boundary (a)", "Bias (z)", "Non-decision time (t0)"))
      re_df <- re_df %>% filter(!is.na(parameter))
      if (nrow(re_df) > 0) {
        p_re <- ggplot(re_df, aes(x = parameter, y = estimate, fill = parameter)) +
          geom_violin(alpha = 0.3, trim = FALSE) +
          geom_boxplot(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.7, outlier.shape = NA) +
          geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50", linewidth = 0.5) +
          scale_fill_manual(values = c("Drift (v)" = "#2E86AB", "Boundary (a)" = "#A23B72", "Bias (z)" = "#28A745", "Non-decision time (t0)" = "#6C757D"), guide = "none") +
          labs(title = "Subject-Level Parameter Estimates (Random Effects)", subtitle = "Individual differences in DDM parameters",
               x = "DDM Parameter", y = "Random Effect Estimate (link scale)", fill = "Parameter") +
          theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
          theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5), legend.position = "none", panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
        print(p_re)
      } else { include_graphics_safe(fig_path("fig_subject_parameter_distribution.pdf")) }
      } else { include_graphics_safe(fig_path("fig_subject_parameter_distribution.pdf")) }
    } else { include_graphics_safe(fig_path("fig_subject_parameter_distribution.pdf")) }
  }, error = function(e) { include_graphics_safe(fig_path("fig_subject_parameter_distribution.pdf")) })
} else {
include_graphics_safe(fig_path("fig_subject_parameter_distribution.pdf"))
}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-parameter-correlation
#| fig-cap: "Subject-Level Parameter Correlation: Drift Intercept vs. Bias Intercept. Scatter plot showing the relationship between subject-level drift intercept and bias intercept estimates. Each point represents one subject (n = 67). The correlation is $r$ = -0.205, indicating a weak negative relationship: subjects with stronger negative drift (toward 'Same') tend to have slightly lower bias (closer to 0.5, less bias toward 'Different'). The regression line with 95% confidence interval (shaded ribbon) shows the trend. This pattern suggests that participants who are more sensitive to stimulus identity (stronger negative drift) may also adopt more neutral starting points, potentially reflecting a more conservative decision strategy."
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-pos: "htbp"
#| out-width: "70%"
# Dynamic: from model coef when brms available
model_path_cor <- file.path(proj_root, params$run_dir, "models", "additive__probe_onset_locked__thr0.20.rds")
if (file.exists(model_path_cor) && requireNamespace("brms", quietly = TRUE)) {
  tryCatch({
    suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(brms))
    fit_cor <- readRDS(model_path_cor)
    coef_subj <- coef(fit_cor, summary = TRUE)
    if (!is.null(coef_subj) && "subject_id" %in% names(coef_subj)) {
      drift_coefs <- coef_subj$subject_id[, , "Intercept"]
      bias_coefs <- coef_subj$subject_id[, , "bias_Intercept"]
      if (!is.null(drift_coefs) && !is.null(bias_coefs)) {
        subj_cor <- tibble(subject_id = rownames(drift_coefs), drift_intercept = drift_coefs[, "Estimate"], bias_intercept = bias_coefs[, "Estimate"])
        cor_val <- cor(subj_cor$drift_intercept, subj_cor$bias_intercept, use = "complete.obs")
        p_cor <- ggplot(subj_cor, aes(x = drift_intercept, y = bias_intercept)) +
          geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.7, color = "#1f78b4") +
          geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, color = "#DC143C", linewidth = 1.2, fill = "gray90", alpha = 0.3) +
          labs(title = "Subject-Level Parameter Correlation", subtitle = sprintf("Drift Intercept vs. Bias Intercept (r = %.3f)", cor_val),
               x = "Drift Intercept (Subject-Level)", y = "Bias Intercept (Subject-Level, logit scale)") +
          theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
          theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5), plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5, color = "gray50"))
        print(p_cor)
      } else { include_graphics_safe(fig_path("plot4_parameter_correlation.png")) }
    } else { include_graphics_safe(fig_path("plot4_parameter_correlation.png")) }
  }, error = function(e) { include_graphics_safe(fig_path("plot4_parameter_correlation.png")) })
} else {
include_graphics_safe(fig_path("plot4_parameter_correlation.png"))
}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-brinley-plot
#| fig-cap: "Brinley Plot: Reaction Time Relationships. Scatter plot showing mean RT for Hard trials (y-axis) versus Easy trials (x-axis) for each participant, colored by effort condition (blue = Low effort, crimson = High effort). Reaction times are displayed in milliseconds (ms). The dashed diagonal line (slope = 1) represents proportional slowing (equal RT increase in both conditions). The solid black regression line shows the actual relationship with 95% confidence interval (shaded ribbon), with slope > 1 indicating disproportionate slowing in Hard trials relative to Easy trials. Points above the diagonal indicate participants who slowed more in Hard relative to Easy trials. This visualization connects our DDM findings to the broader cognitive aging literature on generalized slowing [@brinley1965cognitive; @cerella1985; @salthouse1996]."
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-pos: "htbp"
#| out-width: "70%"
# Dynamic: computed from behavioral_data
if (!is.null(behavioral_data) && nrow(behavioral_data) > 0) {
  subj_col <- intersect(c("subject_id", "sub"), names(behavioral_data))[1]
  rt_col <- intersect(c("rt", "same_diff_resp_secs", "resp1RT"), names(behavioral_data))[1]
  diff_col <- intersect(c("difficulty_level", "difficulty"), names(behavioral_data))[1]
  effort_col <- intersect(c("effort_condition", "effort"), names(behavioral_data))[1]
  if (!is.null(subj_col) && !is.null(rt_col) && !is.null(diff_col) && !is.null(effort_col)) {
    brinley_data <- behavioral_data %>%
      filter(!is.na(!!sym(rt_col)), !!sym(rt_col) > 0, !!sym(rt_col) < 10,
             !is.na(!!sym(diff_col)), !is.na(!!sym(effort_col))) %>%
      group_by(!!sym(subj_col), !!sym(diff_col), !!sym(effort_col)) %>%
      summarise(mean_rt = mean(!!sym(rt_col), na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
      pivot_wider(names_from = !!sym(diff_col), values_from = mean_rt, names_prefix = "mean_rt_")
    if ("mean_rt_Easy" %in% names(brinley_data) && "mean_rt_Hard" %in% names(brinley_data)) {
      brinley_plot_data <- brinley_data %>%
        filter(!is.na(mean_rt_Easy), !is.na(mean_rt_Hard)) %>%
        mutate(
          mean_rt_Easy_ms = mean_rt_Easy * 1000,
          mean_rt_Hard_ms = mean_rt_Hard * 1000,
          effort = !!sym(effort_col)
        )
      effort_levs <- unique(brinley_plot_data$effort)
      high_eff <- effort_levs[grepl("High|40", as.character(effort_levs), ignore.case = TRUE)][1]
      low_eff  <- effort_levs[grepl("Low|5", as.character(effort_levs), ignore.case = TRUE)][1]
      if (is.na(high_eff)) high_eff <- effort_levs[1]
      if (is.na(low_eff))  low_eff <- effort_levs[length(effort_levs)]
      color_map <- setNames(c("#DC143C", "#1E90FF"), c(as.character(high_eff), as.character(low_eff)))
      fit_line <- lm(mean_rt_Hard_ms ~ mean_rt_Easy_ms, data = brinley_plot_data)
      slope <- coef(fit_line)[2]
      p_brinley <- ggplot(brinley_plot_data, aes(x = mean_rt_Easy_ms, y = mean_rt_Hard_ms)) +
        geom_point(aes(color = effort), size = 2.5, alpha = 0.7) +
        geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50", linewidth = 0.5) +
        geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, color = "black", linewidth = 1, alpha = 0.2) +
        scale_color_manual(values = color_map, labels = c("High Effort", "Low Effort")) +
        labs(title = "Brinley Plot: Reaction Time Relationships",
             subtitle = sprintf("Easy vs. Hard difficulty (slope = %.2f)", slope),
             x = "Mean RT: Easy Trials (ms)", y = "Mean RT: Hard Trials (ms)", color = "Effort Condition") +
        theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
        theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 13, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
              plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, hjust = 0.5, color = "gray60"),
              legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
      print(p_brinley)
    } else {
include_graphics_safe(fig_path("fig_brinley_plot.pdf"))
    }
  } else {
    include_graphics_safe(fig_path("fig_brinley_plot.pdf"))
  }
} else {
  include_graphics_safe(fig_path("fig_brinley_plot.pdf"))
}
```

```{r}
    z_q2.5 = round(z_q2.5, 3),
    z_q97.5 = round(z_q97.5, 3),
    `95% CrI` = paste0("[", z_q2.5, ", ", z_q97.5, "]")
  ) %>%
  select(task, effort_condition, z_mean, `95% CrI`) %>%
  rename(
    `Task` = task,
    `Effort` = effort_condition,
    `Mean z` = z_mean
  )

tbl_bias_bycond %>%
  knitr::kable(format = ifelse(knitr::is_latex_output(), "latex", "html"), 
               booktabs = TRUE, 
               linesep = "") %>%
  kableExtra::kable_styling(
    latex_options = c("striped", "hold_position"),
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed", "responsive"),
    full_width = FALSE
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-bias-drift-intercept

if (!is.null(tbl_sob_fixef)) {
  if ("rt_def" %in% names(tbl_sob_fixef) && !"rt_type" %in% names(tbl_sob_fixef)) {
    tbl_sob_fixef <- tbl_sob_fixef %>% rename(rt_type = rt_def)
  }
  drift_intercept_raw <- tbl_sob_fixef %>%
    filter(threshold == PRIMARY_THR, rt_type == PRIMARY_RT) %>%
    filter(term == "Intercept" | term == "(Intercept)") %>%

    { if ("dpar" %in% names(.)) filter(., dpar == "v") else . } %>%
    slice(1)
  if (nrow(drift_intercept_raw) > 0) {
    est_col <- if ("Estimate" %in% names(drift_intercept_raw)) "Estimate" else "estimate"
    q2_col <- if ("Q2.5" %in% names(drift_intercept_raw)) "Q2.5" else if ("q2.5" %in% names(drift_intercept_raw)) "q2.5" else NA_character_
    q97_col <- if ("Q97.5" %in% names(drift_intercept_raw)) "Q97.5" else if ("q97.5" %in% names(drift_intercept_raw)) "q97.5" else NA_character_
    if (is.na(q2_col) || is.na(q97_col)) {

        kableExtra::kable_styling(latex_options = c("hold_position"), full_width = FALSE)
    } else {
      drift_intercept <- drift_intercept_raw %>%

        mutate(
          estimate = round(!!sym(est_col), 3),
          q2.5 = round(!!sym(q2_col), 3),
          q97.5 = round(!!sym(q97_col), 3),

        kableExtra::kable_styling(latex_options = c("striped", "hold_position"), bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed", "responsive"), full_width = FALSE)
    }
  } else {
```

## A3. Posterior Predictive Checks and Diagnostics {#app-ch3-ppc .unnumbered}

**Conditional Accuracy Function (CAF).** The Conditional Accuracy Function (CAF) shows how accuracy varies across RT bins, providing a diagnostic for speed–accuracy tradeoffs. @fig-caf plots empirical accuracy by RT bin for each Task × Effort × Difficulty combination. Consistent with evidence-accumulation dynamics, faster responses (lower RT bins) tend toward chance accuracy, while slower responses show higher accuracy. This pattern validates the DDM's core assumption that decisions improve with longer evidence accumulation times.

```{r}
#| label: fig-caf
#| fig-cap: "Conditional Accuracy Function (CAF). Empirical accuracy by RT bin for each Task × Effort × Difficulty combination. Shows the speed–accuracy tradeoff: faster responses (lower bins) tend toward chance accuracy, while slower responses show higher accuracy, consistent with evidence accumulation over time."
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "85%"
# Dynamic: prefer behavioral_data (fresh on re-render), else load 04_all_caf_empirical.csv
caf_file <- file.path(proj_root, "output/publish/04_all_caf_empirical.csv")
caf_from_behav <- !is.null(behavioral_data) && nrow(behavioral_data) > 0
rt_col <- if (caf_from_behav) intersect(c("rt", "same_diff_resp_secs", "resp1RT"), names(behavioral_data))[1] else NULL
acc_col_behav <- if (caf_from_behav) intersect(c("correct", "iscorr", "accuracy", "resp_is_correct"), names(behavioral_data))[1] else NULL
task_col <- if (caf_from_behav) intersect(c("task", "Task"), names(behavioral_data))[1] else NULL
diff_col <- if (caf_from_behav) intersect(c("difficulty_level", "difficulty"), names(behavioral_data))[1] else NULL
effort_col <- if (caf_from_behav) intersect(c("effort_condition", "effort"), names(behavioral_data))[1] else NULL
caf_from_behav <- caf_from_behav && !is.null(rt_col) && !is.null(acc_col_behav) && !is.null(task_col) && !is.null(diff_col) && !is.null(effort_col)

if (caf_from_behav) {
  caf_computed <- behavioral_data %>%
    filter(!is.na(!!sym(rt_col)), !!sym(rt_col) > 0, !!sym(rt_col) < 10,
           !is.na(!!sym(acc_col_behav)), !is.na(!!sym(task_col)), !is.na(!!sym(diff_col)), !is.na(!!sym(effort_col))) %>%
    mutate(
      task = factor(!!sym(task_col)),
      effort_condition = factor(case_when(grepl("High|40", as.character(!!sym(effort_col))) ~ "High", TRUE ~ "Low"), levels = c("Low", "High")),
      difficulty_level = factor(!!sym(diff_col), levels = c("Standard", "Easy", "Hard"))
    ) %>%
    group_by(task, effort_condition, difficulty_level) %>%
    mutate(bin = cut(!!sym(rt_col), breaks = 5, labels = FALSE)) %>%
    filter(!is.na(bin)) %>%
    group_by(task, effort_condition, difficulty_level, bin) %>%
    summarise(acc_emp = mean(as.numeric(!!sym(acc_col_behav)), na.rm = TRUE), bin_rt_mid = mean(!!sym(rt_col), na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
  if (nrow(caf_computed) > 0) {
    p_caf <- ggplot(caf_computed, aes(x = bin_rt_mid, y = acc_emp)) +
      geom_point(size = 1.6, color = "black") + geom_path(linewidth = 0.7, color = "black", alpha = 0.6) +
      facet_grid(task + effort_condition ~ difficulty_level) +
      labs(x = "RT bin midpoint (s)", y = "Accuracy", title = "Conditional Accuracy Function: Accuracy by RT Bin",
           subtitle = "Empirical accuracy (speed-accuracy tradeoff)") +
      scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
      theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
      theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
            plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, color = "gray50", hjust = 0.5), strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"))
    print(p_caf)
  } else { include_graphics_safe(fig_path("fig_caf.pdf")) }
} else if (file.exists(caf_file)) {
  caf_data <- read_csv(caf_file, show_col_types = FALSE)
  acc_col <- intersect(c("acc_emp", "emp_caf"), names(caf_data))[1]
  bin_col <- intersect(c("bin_rt_mid", "bin"), names(caf_data))[1]
  if (!is.null(acc_col) && !is.null(bin_col)) {
    if (acc_col == "emp_caf") caf_data <- caf_data %>% rename(acc_emp = emp_caf)
    caf_plot <- caf_data %>%
      mutate(
        task = factor(task),
        effort_condition = factor(case_when(grepl("High|40", as.character(effort_condition)) ~ "High", TRUE ~ "Low"), levels = c("Low", "High")),
        difficulty_level = factor(difficulty_level, levels = c("Standard", "Easy", "Hard")),
        bin_rt_mid = as.numeric(!!sym(bin_col))
      ) %>%
      filter(!is.na(acc_emp), is.finite(acc_emp))
    if (nrow(caf_plot) > 0) {
      p_caf <- ggplot(caf_plot, aes(x = bin_rt_mid, y = acc_emp)) +
        geom_point(size = 1.6, color = "black") + geom_path(linewidth = 0.7, color = "black", alpha = 0.6) +
        facet_grid(task + effort_condition ~ difficulty_level) +
        labs(x = "RT bin midpoint (s)", y = "Accuracy", title = "Conditional Accuracy Function: Accuracy by RT Bin",
             subtitle = "Empirical accuracy (speed-accuracy tradeoff)") +
        scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
        theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
        theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
              plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, color = "gray50", hjust = 0.5), strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"))
      print(p_caf)
    } else { include_graphics_safe(fig_path("fig_caf.pdf")) }
  } else { include_graphics_safe(fig_path("fig_caf.pdf")) }
} else {
  include_graphics_safe(fig_path("fig_caf.pdf"))
}
```

**PPC Residual Heatmaps.** PPC residual heatmaps visualize model fit across the 12 experimental cells (Task × Effort × Difficulty). Each cell is colored by two fit metrics: KS statistic (Kolmogorov–Smirnov, comparing RT distributions) and QP RMSE (quantile–probability root-mean-squared error, comparing RT quantiles). Darker red indicates poorer fit. Pre-declared thresholds were KS $<$ 0.15 (warn) and $<$ 0.20 (fail), QP RMSE $<$ 0.09 s (warn) and $<$ 0.12 s (fail). Most cells show acceptable fit (light colors), with notable misfit concentrated in Easy–VDT conditions (darker red), consistent with known fast-tail underfitting in the base Wiener DDM.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ppc-heatmaps
#| fig-cap: "PPC Residual Heatmaps. KS statistic and QP RMSE by Task × Effort × Difficulty for all models (top panel) and primary model only (bottom panel). Darker red indicates larger residuals (poorer fit). The primary model shows acceptable fit across most cells, with notable misfit in Easy/VDT conditions."
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "80%"
include_graphics_safe(fig_path("fig_ppc_heatmaps.pdf"))
```
